doc.title: Derrick Gardner interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 9, 2013

title: Learning the Basie band's way of phrasing and breathing
summary: Gardner is caught out by the band's unwritten phrasing in 'Right On Right On' and 'L'il Darlin'', where everyone breathes as one.

story.theme_name: Playing with Count Basie: joining, leading, leaving
story.community_name: Playing with Count Basie: the band, its feel and its people

blocks.x: Well yeah. I knew some of the music, but the Basie band has their own way of playing what is written on the page, which makes the band sound particularly unique. And for instance there’s a piece in there, an Ernie Wilkins’ piece called “Right On Right On.” © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -5-

And it’s figured a quarter rest followed by four eighth notes, eighth rest, followed by an eighth note tied over. And so I saw it and I said [scats]. So we got to it and this is the B shout section, right, you know. And so we get to it and the whole band goes [scats]. And I’m going [scats].
Do you guys have the same music that I do?

[scats] Okay, wow. But you could say everybody was just kind of looking at me because they knew — they knew coming up to that that there’s no pre-instruction that that’s going to happen. So I’m going [scats] and out of the corner of everybody’s eyes it’s like — like that you know. Well thanks guys for telling me this, you know. And then the hardest piece in the book, I always say this, was “L’il Darlin’” because of the breath control. “L’il Darlin’” and Thad Jones’ piece called “To You.” Both are very similar ballads. With “L’il Darlin’” they have this phrasing and breathing thing in part of the melody where again it’s written one way and it’s played another way. You know the tune is [scats]. You know like that. And so moving on to [scats]. But I’m like [scats]. And I’m looking at the page and I said why that’s a natural breath to take right there. Oh, okay, this is the way that they do it. It totally blew my mind, first that you could do that, and also that everybody in that band breathed and phrased like one person. I mean everybody. And if a new person comes into the band you could tell it, and he or she’s going to be out of place because the phrasing is so exact and so unique. So yeah, that was definitely a revelation in my musical life.
